Hello, I'm Dr. Mark Kovacs excited to be presenting quick tennis research summaries for coaches and really the purpose of this presentation is to summarize three or four relevant areas of research that have been done in the last few years that I thought was really relevant for tennis coaches at all levels of the game. So let's start with the tennis serve. So as the major shot in the game, there's been quite a bit of research in this area and before we get into a couple of the studies that I thought were really interesting, just to remind folks how I evaluated, I go through this eight stage analysis, so eight steps to every serve and then you're looking to see where people fall. What a style versus what a fundamentals and in the couple studies that I'll be talking about, there's a couple really interesting areas related to it and the big ones are take a look at loading stage three, take a look at stage four, which is cocking, and then you have acceleration, contact and deceleration. So as you can see here, we have eight stages. The ones that we're going to be talking about the most today are going to be stages three, four, five and six. So as we go through, just keep that in mind. So a really, really good study, pretty recently done out of a lab in France, Gorsi et al, did a really nice job of trying to analyze slow and fast service. So just comparing people that serve fast and people that don't serve so fast.

Now let's take a look at this really interesting study that was done pretty recently as well in the last year or two. And this is Deng et al. And they looked at the effects of strength and conditioning interventions on serve speed in tennis players. And they did a systematic review with a meta analysis. So a systematic review first off and a meta analysis are sort of two different things. But many times they're done together. A systematic review is analyzing the papers or the research that has been done on a topic using certain criteria. So these researchers looked at all the papers done on training studies and serve speed to see why their relationships. And there were certain criteria that they included and there were certain criteria they excluded. So that's where systematic reviews usually focus and they focus then on looking at the data summarizing the data somewhat as objectively as possible. But there's a little bit of subjectivity to how it is analyzed based on the criteria. Then you add in a meta analysis which is a statistical procedure on top of that that tries to put statistics on studies that were done differently. Which makes it interesting. But you also got to understand the limitations because all these studies were done very, very differently. Some were done in younger kids. Some were done in in college players. Some were done in pros. We've got individuals that are very high level and then individuals that aren't as high level.

So their serve may have still been developing. You've got males. You've got females. You've got different amounts of training time. Different number of serves that people hit. And then you've got very different strength and conditioning interventions. So there's a lot of limitations in studies like this, especially when you're looking at overall strength and conditioning on one variable, which is serve speed. So we just got to be careful on how we interpret it. However, there was some interesting information that big picture I think is important for coaches to understand. One is the definition of training modes is important. As we can see here, you've got resistance training, core training, multimodal, which is pretty much everything. You're doing resistance training, you're doing core training, you're doing plyometrics, you're doing a lot of different things. So that's typically what you would consider a traditional, well structured, semi well structured, strength and conditioning program would be a multimodal training program. So in this definition, it's a combination of at least two forms of strength and conditioning could be strength and speed, strength and power, things like that. Plyometrics, I think most people know that's just the power of the jumping, predominantly jumping type of activities with the lower body. And then you can also do some plyometric throwing activities as well.

So just to be aware of how this was broken down. So this is a chart from the study itself. Don't worry about the information on the left. But what we want to really focus on here is if you look at the blue bars on the right, we're looking at which ones had the biggest effect size. So it's really practically speaking, which ones had the best statistical analysis or would give us the most confidence that the data is good. The bigger the squares, the better from that standpoint. So that, as they say here, the size of the plotted squares reflect the statistical weight of the study. So we're seeing improvements in pretty much all of these. Anything moving to the right, the more to the right, the better, the bigger the improvement on surf speed. So you can kind of see we've got quite a few there that definitely highlight that there is a correlation there or there is a relationship there. So if we're going to summarize this for coaches, what do we need to understand? The findings from these studies indicated that strength and conditioning interventions, specifically multimodal training, enhance surf speed. The training programs that yielded the largest effect size on surf speed, which gave you the biggest bang for the buck, utilized multimodal exercises targeting both upper and lower extremities. So developing a structured strength and conditioning program with an emphasis of improving surf speed can be achieved with off court effective training.

So there's definitely some opportunity here to improve surf speed with off court physical training, well structured strength and conditioning programming and applying it appropriately.

So this study was looking at shoulder range of motion and competitive tennis players and what happens to shoulder range of motion. Having anything over 20 studies is really positive, really, really helpful. So as you can see here, we've got these dominant and non-dominant sides looking at the range of motion. So when you're comparing dominant and non-dominant shoulders, that's typically what we do. We have a control group in tennis most of the time, because most people's dominant shoulder have significant differences than the non-dominant due to serving and even due to forehand, a little bit due to backhand, but mainly due to forehand. So some of the biggest takeaways here that I think are really important that all coaches should be aware of, that if you pull all these studies together, it doesn't matter age, gender, you just pull them together. They reveal that the dominant shoulders had significant less, so smaller, internal rotation range of motion. So 53 degrees on average compared to 63 degrees on average. So you've got a 10 degree difference between the dominant side and the non-dominant side in the negative. So if they're right-handed, their internal shoulder rotation on the right-hand side is about 10 degrees worse than the left.
